title: Writing Formally
overview: Formality is five separate dials, not one switch, and turning them all at once is what makes official writing unreadable. Acknowledge something without promising anything. Fix the order of events so nobody can reconstruct it differently. Then find the plain twin of every formal word, and keep the one that has none.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an account of a rewritten letter, a guide to official writing, and a formal letter.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Write formally and still be understood the first time
Write an account whose order cannot be reconstructed differently
Join two formal statements so the relation is exact
Read a legal phrase and say what it means plainly
Write a decision so the person affected knows what to do
Open and close a letter correctly
lectureScript:
This unit is about formality, and it starts by disagreeing with something most people believe about it.
Formality is not a switch. It is five separate dials, and you can set each one on its own.

The first dial is contractions. We have not, rather than we haven't. That one is nearly free: turn it up in anything official.
The second is vocabulary. Enquire rather than ask. Notify rather than tell. Forward rather than send on. This one has a cost, because the formal word is usually the less familiar one.
The third is the passive, and whether you name a person. Your form has been received, rather than we got your form.
The fourth is sentence length, and how many clauses you put in one sentence.
The fifth is distance from the reader. You, then applicants, then the undersigned.
Almost all bad official writing comes from turning all five to maximum at once.
And the damage is done by the last two. A thirty-word sentence loses the reader. The undersigned makes a letter cold.
Most good professional writing sits about three out of five on the first three dials, and low on the last two.
That combination has a name, and the name is plain English.
Plain does not mean informal. A document can be entirely formal and still be understood the first time, and that is the whole target of this unit.

The reading makes that concrete. Somebody spent two years rewriting the letters a housing office sent.
The first one they were given contained pursuant, aforementioned, notwithstanding and therein, and it was entirely correct.
They gave it to eight tenants. Two understood it. Three understood part of it. Three thought it said the opposite.
That third group is the point, because the letter was a deadline and they had missed it.
Half the office thought making it plainer would make it sound careless. It did not.
The rewrite kept the passive, kept the absence of contractions, and kept four sentences. Three dials stayed up.
What it dropped was the vocabulary nobody outside the office used, and one relative clause thirty words long.
Eight out of eight understood the new one.

The second card is the verb of formal correspondence, and you have had the form since Unit 10.
Your application has been received. The matter has been referred. Your letter has been forwarded.
Why the passive? Not vagueness. We have received your application says a person did it, and invites the question which person. The passive states the position of the organisation.
Why the perfect rather than the past simple? Because was received closes the subject, and has been received says it happened and still stands.
And here is the honest thing about all of them. None of them promises anything.
Has been received, has been referred, has been noted. All true, and none of them says anybody will act.
So when you write one, ask whether you meant to commit. If you did, add a name or a date, because that is what turns an acknowledgement into an answer.
And when you receive one, the useful question is what will happen, and by when.

The third card is the past perfect passive, doing the job it exists for.
A formal account has three layers, and each takes its own tense.
The past perfect for what was already true. The past simple for what then happened. The present perfect for what stands now.
The application had been forwarded in March. No acknowledgement was received. The matter has since been escalated.
Three sentences, three tenses, and the order is now beyond dispute, which is the whole reason for writing an account at all.
The error is the one from Unit 10. Do not drop the been. The letter had forwarded says the letter did the forwarding.

The fourth card completes something from Unit 1.
Unit 1 gave you the which that points back at a whole clause. It is one member of a family.
In which case, for a condition. At which point, for a moment. As a result of which, for a cause. For which reason, for a consequence. By which time, for a span.
Each takes a comma in front and a full clause after, and each says something slightly different.
They are formal, so keep them for accounts and reports. In an email, so and then will do.

The last card sorts the formal vocabulary into two piles.
Most of it has a plain twin. Notwithstanding is despite. Pursuant to is under. Aforementioned is that. Therein is in it. Prior to is before.
Where a plain twin exists, use it, unless you are inside a contract.
One word has no twin at all, and it is worth knowing why.
Hereby. I hereby confirm that the work is complete.
That sentence does not describe a confirmation. It IS the confirmation. The saying is the act.
Which is why you cannot write I hereby went, and why the person rewriting those letters kept I hereby give notice word for word.
It was the only phrase in the whole letter that was doing a job no plain phrase could do.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: Used to close a letter that opened with a name.
words.example: Dear Ms Adeyemi ... Yours sincerely.
practice: Yours sincerely follows a named person.
Yours faithfully follows Dear Sir or Madam.
Getting the pair wrong is noticed in Britain and nowhere else.
Its adjective is sincere.
words.tutor: Close a letter correctly. Ask the tutor to check it against the opening.

words.meaning: Used to close a letter to somebody unnamed.
words.example: Dear Sir or Madam ... Yours faithfully.
practice: Faithfully goes with an unnamed opening.
If you know the name, use it, and close with sincerely.
In an email, Kind regards replaces both.
The pair is British: other countries differ.
words.tutor: Close an unnamed letter. Ask the tutor which opening it belongs to.

words.meaning: Included with a letter, in the same envelope.
words.example: Please find enclosed a copy of the invoice.
practice: Enclosed is for a letter; attached is for an email.
Please find enclosed is old-fashioned and still standard.
I enclose is shorter and equally correct.
Its noun is an enclosure.
words.tutor: Enclose something. Ask the tutor about enclosed and attached.

words.meaning: With this letter; along with this.
words.example: I forward herewith the signed agreement.
practice: Herewith is very formal and slightly archaic.
It means the same as enclosed.
It is one word: here plus with.
In most letters, with this is better.
words.tutor: Use herewith. Ask the tutor whether a plainer word would have been better.

words.meaning: The person who has signed below.
words.example: The undersigned confirms receipt.
practice: The undersigned is a way of saying I without saying I.
It takes the, always.
It is legal register and rare elsewhere.
It is one word.
words.tutor: Use the undersigned. Ask the tutor what it is avoiding.

words.meaning: Letters and emails, taken together.
words.example: All correspondence should be sent to the address below.
practice: Correspondence is uncountable.
It covers the whole exchange, not one letter.
Its verb is correspond, which takes with.
It also means a match between two things.
words.tutor: Direct correspondence somewhere. Ask the tutor to check the plural.

words.meaning: To ask, formally.
words.example: I am writing to enquire about the vacancy.
practice: Enquire is the formal ask.
It takes about, or whether.
Its noun is an enquiry.
Inquire, with an i, is the American spelling and the investigative one.
words.starter: I am writing to enquire about …
words.tutor: Enquire about something. Ask the tutor about enquire and inquire.

words.meaning: To tell somebody officially.
words.example: You will be notified within ten working days.
practice: Notify takes a person, and of for the thing.
It is very common in the passive.
Its noun is notification, from Unit 16.
Notifying is official; telling is not.
words.tutor: Write a notification line. Ask the tutor to check the preposition.

words.meaning: To send something on to somebody else.
words.example: Your letter has been forwarded to the relevant department.
practice: Forward takes to.
It is very common in the perfect passive.
Forwarding passes it on; it does not answer it.
It is also an adjective and an adverb.
words.tutor: Report forwarding something. Ask the tutor whether it answered anything.

words.meaning: To add something at the end of a document.
words.example: A copy of the schedule is appended.
practice: Append takes to.
Its noun is an appendix, plural appendices.
Appending adds at the end; enclosing puts it in the envelope.
It is formal and belongs to reports.
words.tutor: Append something. Ask the tutor about append and enclose.

words.meaning: To do what a rule or an instruction requires.
words.example: The work complies with the specification.
practice: Comply always takes with.
Its noun is compliance, from Unit 10.
Complying is doing what is required, not agreeing with it.
Non-compliance is the standard negative.
words.tutor: Report compliance. Ask the tutor to check you said comply WITH.

words.meaning: To stop yourself from doing something.
words.example: Visitors are asked to refrain from smoking.
practice: Refrain takes from plus an -ing form.
It is the formal way of saying do not.
It is almost always used in a request or a notice.
It is also a noun in music, meaning a chorus.
words.tutor: Write a notice with refrain. Ask the tutor to check the form after from.

words.meaning: A short statement of the main points, usually at the front.
words.example: The summary should stand on its own.
practice: A summary comes first and is written last.
An executive summary is the same thing, named for its reader.
Its verb is summarise.
A good summary can be read instead of the report.
words.tutor: Describe a summary. Ask the tutor when it should be written.

words.meaning: The account of how the work was done.
words.example: The methodology explains why those four sites were chosen.
practice: Methodology is the account of the method, strictly.
It exists so a reader can judge the findings.
It is often the shortest section and the most important.
Its adjective is methodological.
words.tutor: Describe a methodology. Ask the tutor what it lets a reader do.

words.meaning: Material placed at the end, outside the main argument.
words.example: The full data is in Appendix B.
practice: Its plural is appendices.
An appendix holds what a reader may want and does not need.
Its verb is append.
If the argument depends on it, it is not an appendix.
words.tutor: Refer to an appendix. Ask the tutor what belongs in one.

words.meaning: A statement of what should be done.
words.example: Each recommendation names who should act and by when.
practice: A recommendation takes that plus a clause, or an -ing form.
Its verb is recommend, from Unit 12.
A recommendation without a name and a date is a wish.
Recommendations usually come last and are read first.
words.tutor: Write a recommendation. Ask the tutor whether it named who and when.

words.meaning: What a piece of work covers.
words.example: Two sites were outside the scope of this review.
practice: Scope takes of.
Scope says what is IN; remit says what you were asked to do.
Out of scope is the standard phrase.
Its verb is to scope a project.
words.tutor: Define a scope. Ask the tutor how it differs from a remit.

words.meaning: The authority and limits given to somebody for a task.
words.example: That question falls outside our remit.
practice: A remit is granted; a scope is chosen.
It is British: mandate is the wider word.
The stress is on the first part for the noun: RE-mit.
Exceeding your remit is a real problem in a report.
words.starter: That falls outside our remit because …
words.tutor: Describe a remit. Ask the tutor how it differs from a scope.

words.meaning: By this document; by saying this.
words.example: I hereby confirm that the work is complete.
practice: Hereby means the saying IS the doing.
It belongs to declarations, not to descriptions.
I hereby confirm is correct; I hereby went is not.
It is one word.
words.tutor: Use hereby in a declaration. Ask the tutor why it cannot describe a past act.

words.meaning: By which; through which.
words.example: There is a scheme whereby costs are shared.
practice: Whereby introduces the means or the arrangement.
It means by which, in one word.
It follows a noun: a scheme whereby, an arrangement whereby.
It is formal and still current.
words.tutor: Use whereby. Ask the tutor what it replaces.

words.meaning: In that place, or in that document.
words.example: The agreement, and the obligations therein, remain in force.
practice: Therein means in it, formally.
It refers back to something just named.
Therein lies the problem is a fixed phrase.
It is archaic outside legal writing.
words.tutor: Use therein. Ask the tutor what it refers back to.

words.meaning: Mentioned earlier in this document.
words.example: The aforementioned clause has been amended.
practice: Aforementioned points back to something already named.
It is one word and very formal.
In most writing, the or that is enough.
Using it where the is enough is the error.
words.tutor: Use aforementioned. Ask the tutor whether the would have done.

words.meaning: In spite of; despite.
words.example: Notwithstanding the delay, the work was completed.
practice: Notwithstanding takes a noun, like despite.
It can also follow its noun: the delay notwithstanding.
It is one word and very formal.
Despite means the same and is readable.
words.tutor: Use notwithstanding. Ask the tutor whether despite would have been better.

words.meaning: In accordance with; following from.
words.example: Pursuant to clause 6, notice has been given.
practice: Pursuant always takes to.
It means under, or in accordance with.
It is legal register and rare elsewhere.
Under clause 6 says the same thing and is shorter.
words.tutor: Use pursuant to. Ask the tutor for the plain version.

words.meaning: Belonging to ordinary conversation.
words.example: That phrase is too colloquial for a report.
practice: Colloquial means spoken, not wrong.
Its noun is a colloquialism.
Colloquial language is right in speech and wrong in a contract.
It is pronounced co-LOH-kwee-al.
words.tutor: Name something colloquial. Ask the tutor whether colloquial means incorrect.

words.meaning: The level of formality a piece of language uses.
words.example: The register slips in the third paragraph.
practice: Register is the whole level, not one word.
A register can be too high as well as too low.
It also means a list, and a verb meaning to record.
Matching the register is what this unit is about.
words.tutor: Describe a register. Ask the tutor whether it can be too high.

words.meaning: Specialist language that outsiders do not share.
words.example: The summary is full of jargon.
practice: Jargon is uncountable.
Jargon is precise among specialists and opaque outside.
It is not the same as formality.
Removing jargon for the wrong reader loses precision.
words.starter: The … is full of jargon about …
words.tutor: Name some jargon. Ask the tutor when jargon is the right choice.

words.meaning: Using far more words than are needed.
words.example: The opening paragraph is verbose.
practice: Verbose means wordy, not formal.
Its noun is verbosity.
Formal writing is often verbose and does not have to be.
It is pronounced ver-BOHS.
words.tutor: Call something verbose. Ask the tutor whether formal means wordy.

words.meaning: Clear and direct, without unnecessary words.
words.example: Plain English is not informal English.
practice: Plain means clear, not casual.
Plain English is a movement in official writing.
A document can be plain and formal at once.
That is the point of this whole unit.
words.tutor: Explain plain English. Ask the tutor whether plain means informal.

grammar.title: The five dials of formality
grammar.explanation:
Formality is not one switch. It is five separate dials, and most learners
turn all five at once, which produces writing that is stiff rather than
professional. Knowing which dial does what lets you be formal and readable
at the same time.
grammar.rule:
DIAL 1 — CONTRACTIONS
  informal: we haven't received it       formal: we have not received it

DIAL 2 — VOCABULARY, mostly Latin against plain English
  ask -> enquire   tell -> notify   send on -> forward   do not -> refrain from

DIAL 3 — THE PASSIVE, and whether a person is named
  we have received your form  ->  your form has been received

DIAL 4 — SENTENCE LENGTH AND CLAUSES
  short and separate  ->  longer, with relative clauses

DIAL 5 — DISTANCE FROM THE READER
  you should  ->  applicants should  ->  the undersigned should

The mistake is turning all five to maximum. Dial 5 at maximum makes a
letter unfriendly; dial 2 at maximum makes it unreadable.
Most professional writing sits at about three out of five on dials 1 to 3
and much lower on 4 and 5.
Plain does not mean informal. A document can be formal and plain at once,
and that is what you are aiming at.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Make this suitable for a letter to a customer you have not met.
'We haven't got your form yet so we can't start.'
1. Dial 1: expand the contractions. We have not, we cannot.
2. Dial 2: got is very plain. received is better, and no further.
3. Dial 3: the passive removes the blame from them. Your form has not been received.
4. Dial 5: leave it low. Keep you, or the letter becomes cold.
Answer: Your form has not yet been received, so we are unable to begin.
Dials 4 and 5 were left alone, which is why it still sounds like a person.
grammar.mistake:
Turning every dial to maximum is the commonest register error at this level.
Too far: The undersigned is in receipt of no correspondence pertaining
to the aforementioned matter, notwithstanding prior requests therein.
Better: We have not received your form, despite two earlier requests.
The second is still formal. It is simply readable as well.
grammar.tip: Five dials, not one switch. Turn dials 1 to 3, and leave 4 and 5 alone.
grammar.practice:
Say which dial each change turns, and whether it improves the sentence.
1. we haven't -> we have not
2. ask -> enquire
3. we have received it -> it has been received
4. you should -> the undersigned should
5. two short sentences joined into one with a relative clause
6. do not -> refrain from
Now rewrite this for a customer, turning only dials 1 to 3.
7. 'We haven't got your form yet so we can't start.'
grammar.answers:
1. Dial 1. Improves it for any formal document.
2. Dial 2. Improves it in a letter; unnecessary in an email.
3. Dial 3. Improves it where blame is not the point.
4. Dial 5. Usually makes it worse: it is cold.
5. Dial 4. Improves it in a report; makes a letter heavier.
6. Dial 2 at maximum. Right on a notice, wrong in a letter.
7. Your form has not yet been received, so we are unable to begin.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Your application has been received
grammar.explanation:
Unit 10 built the present perfect passive. This card is about the one place
it does the most work: formal correspondence, where it acknowledges without
promising anything, and where the active would say more than the writer
wants to say.
grammar.rule:
has or have + BEEN + past participle

Your application has been received.
The matter has been referred to the relevant department.
Your letter has been forwarded.
No decision has been taken.
The necessary checks have been carried out.

WHY THE PASSIVE, and it is not vagueness:
We have received your application says a person did it, and invites the
question which person. The passive states the position of the organisation.

WHY THE PERFECT, rather than the past simple:
Your application was received says it happened and closes the subject.
Your application has been received says it happened AND still stands.
That is what an acknowledgement is for.

AND THE HONEST WARNING: none of these promises anything.
Received, referred, forwarded, noted. All four are true, and none says
anybody will act. The useful question is what will happen, and by when.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Acknowledge an application without promising a decision.
1. The perfect, because it happened and still stands.
2. The passive, because the organisation is answering, not a person.
3. Add the thing that makes it useful: a date.
Answer: Your application has been received and will be considered at the
meeting on 14 August.
Without the second half it is an acknowledgement. With it, it is an answer.
grammar.mistake:
These forms are so standard that they get used where nothing has happened.
Your concerns have been noted is true even if nobody read them.
That is not the writer's fault when they mean it, and it is worth knowing
what the phrase does and does not commit anybody to.
grammar.tip: The perfect passive acknowledges. It does not promise. Add a date if you mean to promise.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each one for formal correspondence.
1. We got your application.
2. We sent your letter to the right department.
3. We haven't decided anything yet.
4. Somebody has done the checks.
5. We've read what you said.
Now answer.
6. Which of your five promises that anybody will act?
7. Add to number 1 the words that would make it a promise.
grammar.answers:
1. Your application has been received.
2. Your letter has been forwarded to the relevant department.
3. No decision has been taken.
4. The necessary checks have been carried out.
5. Your comments have been noted.
6. None of them. All five report a state and commit nobody.
7. ... and will be considered at the meeting on 14 August.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Had been forwarded: the order of events in an account
grammar.explanation:
Units 9 and 10 built the past perfect and its passive. A formal account uses
them for one purpose above all others: to fix the ORDER of what happened,
so that a reader who was not there cannot reconstruct it any other way.
grammar.rule:
had + BEEN + past participle

The letter had been forwarded before the deadline passed.
No reply had been received when the matter was escalated.
The clause had been amended, which nobody had been told.

THE PATTERN OF A FORMAL ACCOUNT, three layers:
past perfect   what was already true
past simple    what then happened
present perfect what stands now

'The application had been forwarded to the northern office in March.
No acknowledgement was received. The matter has since been escalated.'
Three sentences, three tenses, and the order is now beyond dispute.

AND THE ACTIVE, where a person is named on purpose:
The office had already closed the file when the letter arrived.

Watch the same error as in Unit 10: the been is what gets dropped.
had forwarded = somebody did it.
had been forwarded = it was done, by nobody stated.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
These happened in this order: it was forwarded in March; no reply came; it
has now been escalated. Write it so nobody can reorder it.
1. The forwarding came first, and the account starts after it: past perfect.
2. Nobody replied: that is the event of the account, so past simple.
3. The escalation still stands: present perfect.
Answer: The application had been forwarded in March. No acknowledgement was
received. The matter has since been escalated.
Each tense is doing one job, and together they fix the order.
grammar.mistake:
Dropping the been changes who acted, exactly as in Unit 10.
The letter had forwarded = the letter did the forwarding, which is nonsense.
The letter had been forwarded = somebody forwarded it.
It is grammatical either way, which is why proofreading misses it.
grammar.tip: Past perfect for what was already true. Past simple for the event. Present perfect for what stands.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right form.
1. The letter ___ (forward, passive) before the deadline passed.
2. No reply ___ (receive, passive) when the matter was escalated.
3. The matter ___ (escalate, passive) since, and still stands.
4. The office ___ (already close) the file when the letter arrived. (active)
5. The clause ___ (amend, passive), which nobody ___ (tell, passive).
Now write the three-sentence account.
6. Forwarded in March; no reply; escalated, and it still stands.
Now correct this.
7. The letter had forwarded to the northern office.
grammar.answers:
1. had been forwarded  2. had been received  3. has been escalated
4. had already closed  5. had been amended / had been told
6. The application had been forwarded in March. No acknowledgement was received.
   The matter has since been escalated.
7. had BEEN forwarded. As written, the letter did the forwarding.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: In which case, at which point
grammar.explanation:
Unit 1 of this level gave you the which that points back at a whole clause.
That was one member of a family, and at Stage 9 you need the rest.
Each of them attaches a whole clause to everything that came before it,
and each attaches it differently.
grammar.rule:
WHICH alone — a comment on what you just said:
The clause had been amended, which nobody had been told.

IN WHICH CASE — if that turns out to be so, then:
The parts may be delayed, in which case the work will be rescheduled.

AT WHICH POINT — and at that moment:
No reply was received by the 14th, at which point the matter was escalated.

AS A RESULT OF WHICH — and that caused:
The station was relocated, as a result of which the series is not comparable.

FOR WHICH REASON — and therefore:
The estimate was not binding, for which reason the invoice stands.

BY WHICH TIME — and by then:
The file was reopened in June, by which time two years had passed.

All of them take a COMMA in front and a full clause after.
And all of them are formal: in speech you would use so, and then, or which
meant that.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Join these: no reply was received by the 14th; the matter was escalated at
that moment.
1. What is the link? Not cause, and not a condition. A moment in time.
2. The moment connector is at which point.
3. It takes a comma in front and a full clause after.
Answer: No reply was received by the 14th, at which point the matter was escalated.
As a result of which would claim the escalation was caused by the silence,
which is probably true and is a bigger claim than you needed to make.
grammar.mistake:
These are formal, and learners who meet them use them in emails.
Stiff: Your form arrived on Tuesday, at which point it was passed to me.
Better: Your form arrived on Tuesday and was passed to me.
Keep them for accounts and reports, where the precision earns its weight.
grammar.tip: Each one attaches a clause to everything before it. Choose by the link: time, cause, condition or comment.
grammar.practice:
Join each pair with the right connector.
1. The parts may be delayed. The work will then be rescheduled.
2. No reply came by the 14th. The matter was escalated at that moment.
3. The station was relocated. The series is therefore not comparable.
4. The estimate was not binding. The invoice therefore stands.
5. The file was reopened in June. Two years had passed by then.
6. The clause had been amended. Nobody had been told this.
Now answer.
7. Which of your six would you NOT write in an email, and what would you write?
grammar.answers:
1. ... in which case the work will be rescheduled.
2. ... at which point the matter was escalated.
3. ... as a result of which the series is not comparable.
4. ... for which reason the invoice stands.
5. ... by which time two years had passed.
6. ... which nobody had been told.
7. All of them, in an ordinary email. Use so, and then, or which meant that.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Hereby, whereby, pursuant: the words with no plain twin
grammar.explanation:
Most formal words have an everyday equivalent, and choosing the formal one is
a matter of register. A few do not, and those are worth separating out,
because the rule for them is different: use them only where the document is
genuinely legal, and recognise them everywhere.
grammar.rule:
THE ONES WITH A PLAIN TWIN — usually prefer the twin:
notwithstanding = despite        pursuant to = under
aforementioned  = the, or that   herewith = with this
therein         = in it          prior to = before

THE ONE WITH NO TWIN, because it does what no plain word does:
HEREBY — it makes the saying itself the act.
  I hereby confirm that the work is complete.
  I hereby give notice of my intention to terminate.
That sentence does not describe a confirmation. It IS one.
Which is why you cannot write I hereby went, or I hereby think.

WHEREBY — no single-word twin, though by which comes close.

THE TEST for all the others: write the plain version beside it. If it says
the same thing, use it, unless the document is a contract.
Pursuant to clause 6 and under clause 6 mean the same, and one of them can
be read by the person it applies to.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Improve this for a letter: Pursuant to the aforementioned agreement, and
notwithstanding the obligations therein, notice is hereby given.
1. pursuant to = under. Plain twin exists, so use it.
2. aforementioned = that. Twin exists.
3. notwithstanding = despite. Twin exists.
4. therein = in it. Twin exists.
5. hereby has no twin, and this IS a notice, so it stays.
Answer: Under that agreement, and despite the obligations in it, notice is
hereby given.
One formal word survived, and it survived because it is doing a job.
grammar.mistake:
Learners use these to sound professional, and they achieve the opposite.
Nobody outside a law office writes aforementioned, and a reader who meets it
in a letter assumes the writer is copying a template.
Learn them to READ contracts. Write them only inside one.
grammar.tip: If a plain twin exists, use the twin. hereby is the exception: it does something no other word does.
grammar.practice:
Write the plain twin.
1. notwithstanding  2. pursuant to  3. aforementioned  4. herewith
5. therein  6. prior to
Now answer.
7. Which word in the list has no plain twin, and why?
8. Rewrite for a letter: 'Pursuant to the aforementioned agreement, and
   notwithstanding the obligations therein, notice is hereby given.'
9. Why is 'I hereby went to the meeting' impossible?
grammar.answers:
1. despite  2. under  3. that, or the  4. with this  5. in it  6. before
7. hereby. It makes the saying itself the act, and no plain word does that.
8. Under that agreement, and despite the obligations in it, notice is hereby given.
9. hereby only works where the sentence performs the act. You cannot perform
   a past action by saying it now.
7 or more right: good.

readings.title: The Letter That Nobody Could Read
readings.setting: A housing office, told by somebody who rewrites letters
readings.passage:
My job for two years was rewriting the letters we send, and the first one I was given was a masterpiece.
It was four sentences long and it contained pursuant, aforementioned, notwithstanding and therein.
It was also entirely correct. Every word in it meant what the writer intended.
What we did was give it to eight tenants and ask them what it said.
Two got it right. Three got it partly right. Three thought it said the opposite.
The one that mattered was the third group, because the letter was a deadline and they had missed it.
So we rewrote it, and the argument about the rewrite taught me more than the rewrite did.
Half the office thought making it plainer meant making it informal, and that we would sound careless.
It does not, and we did not. Plain is not the same as casual.
The rewritten version still used the passive, still had no contractions, and still ran to four sentences.
What it dropped was the vocabulary nobody outside the office used, and one relative clause that ran to thirty words.
Eight out of eight got the new one right.
The sentence I kept, word for word, was the one that began I hereby give notice.
That phrase is doing a job no plain phrase does, and it was the only one in the letter that was.

readings.title: Formality Has Five Dials
readings.setting: A page from a guide to official writing
readings.passage:
Most people treat formality as a single switch, and turn it fully on when a document feels important.
It is better understood as five separate dials, each of which can be set on its own.
The first is contractions. We have not, rather than we haven't. This one is nearly free: turn it up in anything official.
The second is vocabulary. Enquire rather than ask, notify rather than tell. This one has a cost, because the formal word is usually the less familiar one.
The third is the passive, and whether a person is named. Your form has been received rather than we got your form.
The fourth is sentence length and the number of clauses in one sentence.
The fifth is distance from the reader. You, then applicants, then the undersigned.
Almost all bad official writing comes from turning all five to maximum at once.
Dials four and five are where the damage is done. A thirty-word sentence loses the reader, and the undersigned makes a letter cold.
Most good professional writing sits about three out of five on the first three dials, and low on the last two.
That combination has a name. It is plain English, and it is not informal English.
A document can be entirely formal and still be understood the first time.

readings.title: Letter: Outstanding Application, Ref HA-2291
readings.setting: A letter from a housing office
readings.passage:
Dear Ms Okonkwo

Application HA-2291: outstanding documents

Your application has been received and has been referred to the assessment team.

Two documents have not yet been received. Your form was forwarded to us on 3 March,
at which point the supporting documents should also have been supplied.
No further correspondence had been received from you when the file was reviewed on 2 April,
for which reason the application has been placed on hold.

Please supply the two documents listed overleaf by 30 April. If they cannot be supplied
by that date, please notify us in writing, in which case the file will be held open for
a further month.

I enclose a copy of the original acknowledgement for your records.

No decision has been taken on your application, and none will be taken until the file is complete.

I hereby confirm that the application will not be closed before 30 May.

Yours sincerely
R. Balewa, Assessment Team

comprehension.q: Of eight tenants, how many understood the original letter correctly?
comprehension.a: Two. Three were partly right and three thought it said the opposite.
comprehension.why: Stated directly, and the third group had missed a deadline as a result.

comprehension.a: No. Every word in it meant what the writer intended.
comprehension.why: The text says it was entirely correct, which is why the failure is a register failure.

comprehension.q: What did the rewritten version keep, and what did it drop?
comprehension.a: It kept the passive, the absence of contractions and the four sentences. It dropped the unfamiliar vocabulary and a thirty-word relative clause.
comprehension.why: That is the point: three dials stayed up and two came down.

comprehension.q: Why was 'I hereby give notice' kept word for word?
comprehension.a: It does a job no plain phrase does.
comprehension.why: hereby makes the saying itself the act, and nothing else in the letter was doing that.

comprehension.a: Contractions; vocabulary; the passive and whether a person is named; sentence length; distance from the reader.
comprehension.why: Listed in order in the article.

comprehension.q: Which two dials does the article say do the damage, and why?
comprehension.a: The fourth and fifth. A thirty-word sentence loses the reader, and 'the undersigned' makes a letter cold.
comprehension.why: The article recommends keeping those two low even in formal writing.

comprehension.q: What does the article say plain English is not?
comprehension.why: A document can be entirely formal and still be understood the first time.

comprehension.q: Has any decision been made on the application?
comprehension.a: No, and none will be until the file is complete.
comprehension.why: Stated in the perfect passive, which reports the position without promising a timetable.

comprehension.q: You cannot supply the documents by 30 April. What should you do, and what follows?
comprehension.a: Notify them in writing, in which case the file is held open for a further month.
comprehension.why: The condition and its consequence are joined by in which case.

comprehension.q: Why does the letter say 'I hereby confirm' in the second-to-last line?
comprehension.a: Because that sentence IS the confirmation, not a report of one.
comprehension.why: It is the one commitment in the letter, and hereby is what makes the saying the act.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Turn three dials, not five
speaking.instructions:
Say each informal sentence aloud, then say it again for a letter to a stranger.
Turn dials one to three. Leave four and five alone.
1. We haven't got your form yet so we can't start.
2. I'm writing to ask about the job.
3. We've sent your letter on to the right people.
4. We haven't decided anything yet.
5. Don't smoke in here.
A model for the first one:
Your form has not yet been received, so we are unable to begin.
Tap the mic. Say all five pairs. Tap again and listen.
Check: did you keep the word you anywhere it was natural?
If every sentence lost its person, dial five went up by mistake.
speaking.tutor: Say your five formal versions and ask the tutor whether any sounded cold.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — The two weak words in the middle
speaking.instructions:
Formal correspondence stacks unstressed words before the main one, and a
listener needs to hear them to know which tense you used.
Listen and repeat. The capitals show the stress.
has been reCEIVED     sounds like  z-bin-reCEIVED
had been forWARDED    sounds like  d-bin-forWARDED
have not been reCEIVED sounds like  v-not-bin-reCEIVED
will be conSIDered    sounds like  l-bee-conSIDered
Now say these three lines.
Your application has been received and has been referred to the team.
No correspondence had been received when the file was reviewed.
No decision has been taken, and none will be taken until the file is complete.
Tap the mic. Say the three lines. Tap again and listen.
Check: can you hear the difference between has been and had been?
One says it stands now. The other says it was already so.
speaking.tutor: Say the three lines and ask the tutor whether it could hear has against had.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Acknowledge without promising
speaking.instructions:
Say each one as formal correspondence would.
1. We got your application.
2. We sent your letter to the right department.
3. We haven't decided anything yet.
4. Somebody has done the checks.
5. We've read what you said.
Models: Your application has been received. Your comments have been noted.
Now say number 1 again, adding the words that would make it a promise.
Tap the mic. Say all five and the promise version. Tap again and listen.
Check: do any of your first five actually commit anybody to anything?
They should not. That is what the form is for.
speaking.tutor: Say your five and ask the tutor which one a reader would mistake for a promise.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: eight tenants
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
My job for two years was rewriting the letters we send.
The first one I was given was four sentences long and contained pursuant,
aforementioned, notwithstanding and therein.
It was also entirely correct. Every word meant what the writer intended.
We gave it to eight tenants and asked them what it said.
Two got it right. Three got it partly right. Three thought it said the opposite.
The third group mattered, because the letter was a deadline and they had missed it.
Half the office thought making it plainer meant making it informal. It does not.
The rewritten version still used the passive, still had no contractions, and still ran to four sentences.
Eight out of eight got the new one right.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. How many of the eight understood the original?
2. Was the original letter incorrect?
3. What did the rewrite keep?
4. What did half the office wrongly believe?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 two, with three partly right. 2 no, it was entirely correct.
3 the passive, no contractions, four sentences. 4 that plainer meant informal.
speaking.tutor: Retell what the rewrite changed and what it kept, in three sentences.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Join it formally
speaking.instructions:
Join each pair aloud with the right formal connector.
1. The parts may be delayed. The work will then be rescheduled.
2. No reply came by the 14th. The matter was escalated at that moment.
3. The station was relocated. The series is therefore not comparable.
4. The estimate was not binding. The invoice therefore stands.
5. The file was reopened in June. Two years had passed by then.
Models: in which case, at which point, as a result of which,
for which reason, by which time.
Tap the mic. Say all five. Tap again and listen.
Check: did you pause at the comma before each connector?
Now say number 2 as you would in an email, and hear how much lighter it is.
speaking.tutor: Say your five and ask the tutor which would be too heavy for an email.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: explain a decision
speaking.instructions:
Explain a decision to somebody affected by it, for two minutes, as you would
on the telephone rather than in writing.
Cover these five, in this order:
what has been received and what has not
what had already happened before the file was looked at
why the decision went as it did
what the person must do, and by when
what will happen if they cannot
Keep dials four and five LOW: short sentences, and say you.
Keep dials one to three up: no contractions, formal verbs, the passive.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: would somebody hearing this once know what to do?
Did any sentence run past about twenty words?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your explanation and ask whether a listener would know what to do.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Turn the dials, one at a time
writing.prompt:
Take this sentence: 'We haven't got your form yet so we can't start.'
Write five versions, turning one more dial each time, and label each with
the dial you turned.
Then write one line saying which version you would actually send, and to whom.
writing.model:
1. (dial 1) We have not got your form yet, so we cannot start.
2. (dial 2) We have not received your form yet, so we are unable to begin.
3. (dial 3) Your form has not yet been received, so work is unable to begin.
4. (dial 4) Your form, which was due on 3 March and has not yet been received,
   means that work is unable to begin.
5. (dial 5) The applicant's form, not having been received, precludes
   commencement of the assessment.

I would send version 3 to a customer. Versions 4 and 5 are worse, not more formal.
writing.criteria:
Five versions, each turning exactly one more dial.
Each labelled with the dial it turned.
Versions 4 and 5 identified as worse rather than more formal.
The final line names a reader, not a preference.
writing.support: Change one thing at a time and read each version aloud before writing the next.
writing.extension: Write the version you would put in a text message, and say which dials you turned down.

writing.title: Writing 2 — An acknowledgement that promises nothing, then one that does
writing.prompt:
Part one. Write six lines of formal acknowledgement, all in the present
perfect passive, that commit nobody to anything.
Part two. Rewrite three of them so they DO commit, by adding a name, a date
or a number.
Part three. Write one line saying what the difference is.
writing.model:
Your application has been received.
The matter has been referred to the assessment team.
Your letter has been forwarded.
No decision has been taken.
Your comments have been noted.
The necessary checks have been carried out.

Your application has been received and will be considered on 14 August.
The matter has been referred to R. Balewa, who will reply within ten working days.
No decision has been taken, and none will be taken before 30 May.

The grammar is identical. What changed is that somebody can now be held to it.
writing.criteria:
Six perfect passives in part one, none of them committing anybody.
Three rewrites, each adding a name, a date or a number.
No been dropped anywhere.
The closing line says the grammar did not change.
writing.support: Write part one first without thinking about part two. The gap will show itself.
writing.extension: Write the reply you would send to an acknowledgement from part one, asking for what part two supplies.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A three-layer account
writing.prompt:
Write a formal account of a case, in about 90 words, using three tenses
deliberately:
past perfect for what was already true, past simple for what happened,
present perfect for what stands now.
Use the passive throughout except where naming a person matters.
Invent the case.
writing.model:
The application had been forwarded to the northern office on 3 March.
The supporting documents had not been supplied at that time.
No acknowledgement was received, and the file was reviewed on 2 April.
The assessment team then placed the application on hold.
The matter has since been escalated, and the file has been reopened.
No decision has been taken.
writing.criteria:
At least two past perfect passives, both for what was already true.
At least two past simple events.
At least two present perfects for what stands now.
No been dropped; a reader could reconstruct the order without being told it.
writing.support: Draw a timeline first, with a line marking where the account starts. Everything above it takes had.
writing.extension: Write the one sentence somebody could dispute, and the document you would cite to support it.

writing.title: Writing 4 — A formal letter
writing.prompt:
Write a formal letter of about 170 words, in the style of Reading 3.
Open with a name and close correctly.
Use the present perfect passive at least three times, and the past perfect
passive at least once.
Use at least two of: in which case, at which point, for which reason,
by which time, as a result of which.
Use hereby exactly once, and only where the sentence performs an act.
Keep every sentence under about twenty-five words.
writing.model:
Dear Ms Okonkwo
Application HA-2291: outstanding documents
Your application has been received and has been referred to the assessment team.
Two documents have not yet been received. Your form was forwarded to us on 3 March,
at which point the supporting documents should also have been supplied.
No further correspondence had been received when the file was reviewed on 2 April,
for which reason the application has been placed on hold.
Please supply the two documents by 30 April. If they cannot be supplied by that date,
please notify us in writing, in which case the file will be held open for a further month.
No decision has been taken, and none will be taken until the file is complete.
I hereby confirm that the application will not be closed before 30 May.
Yours sincerely
writing.criteria:
The closing matches the opening: sincerely for a name, faithfully for none.
Three or more present perfect passives, and one or more past perfect passives.
Two or more formal which connectors, each with a comma in front.
hereby used once, in a sentence that performs an act.
writing.support: Write the facts as six short sentences first. Then join and formalise them.
writing.extension: Give your letter to somebody and ask them what it requires of them. Fix whatever they got wrong.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which dial?
activities.instructions:
Say which of the five dials each change turns, and whether it improves the sentence.
1. we haven't -> we have not
2. ask -> enquire
3. we have received it -> it has been received
4. you should -> the undersigned should
5. two sentences joined with a relative clause
6. do not -> refrain from
7. tell -> notify
8. applicants should -> you should
Now rewrite for a customer, turning only dials 1 to 3.
9. 'We haven't got your form yet so we can't start.'
activities.answers:
1. Dial 1, improves it.  2. Dial 2, improves a letter, unnecessary in an email.
3. Dial 3, improves it where blame is not the point.
4. Dial 5, usually worse: cold.  5. Dial 4, good in a report, heavy in a letter.
6. Dial 2 at maximum: right on a notice, wrong in a letter.
7. Dial 2, improves official writing.  8. Dial 5 turned DOWN, usually better.
9. Your form has not yet been received, so we are unable to begin.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, ask which of the five things changed: contraction, word, voice, length or distance.

activities.title: Practice 2 — The acknowledgement
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each for formal correspondence, in the present perfect passive.
1. We got your application.
2. We sent your letter to the right department.
3. We haven't decided anything yet.
4. Somebody has done the checks.
5. We've read what you said.
6. We've put your file on hold.
Now answer.
7. Which of your six promises that anybody will act?
8. Add to number 1 the words that would make it a promise.
9. Correct: Your application has received.
activities.answers:
1. Your application has been received.
2. Your letter has been forwarded to the relevant department.
3. No decision has been taken.
4. The necessary checks have been carried out.
5. Your comments have been noted.
6. Your file has been placed on hold.
7. None. All six report a state and commit nobody.
8. ... and will be considered at the meeting on 14 August.
9. has BEEN received. Without been it says the application did the receiving.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: After writing each one, ask what a reader could hold you to. The answer should be nothing.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Three layers
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form.
1. The letter ___ (forward, passive) before the deadline passed.
2. No reply ___ (receive, passive) when the matter was escalated.
3. The matter ___ (escalate, passive) since, and still stands.
4. The office ___ (already close) the file when the letter arrived. (active)
5. The clause ___ (amend, passive), which nobody ___ (tell, passive).
6. The file ___ (review, passive) on 2 April. (a single event)
Now write the three-sentence account.
7. Forwarded in March; no reply; escalated, and it still stands.
Now correct this.
8. The letter had forwarded to the northern office.
activities.answers:
1. had been forwarded  2. had been received  3. has been escalated
4. had already closed  5. had been amended / had been told  6. was reviewed
7. The application had been forwarded in March. No acknowledgement was received.
   The matter has since been escalated.
8. had BEEN forwarded.
Number 6 is a single event, so the simple passive, not the perfect.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Draw a timeline with a mark where the account begins. Everything above it takes had.

activities.title: Practice 4 — The formal which
activities.instructions:
Join each pair with the right connector.
1. The parts may be delayed. The work will then be rescheduled.
2. No reply came by the 14th. The matter was escalated at that moment.
3. The station was relocated. The series is therefore not comparable.
4. The estimate was not binding. The invoice therefore stands.
5. The file was reopened in June. Two years had passed by then.
6. The clause had been amended. Nobody had been told this.
7. The documents may not arrive. The file will then be held open.
Now answer.
8. Which would you NOT write in an email, and what would you write instead?
activities.answers:
1. in which case  2. at which point  3. as a result of which
4. for which reason  5. by which time  6. which  7. in which case
8. All of them, in an ordinary email. Use so, and then, or which meant that.
Each takes a comma in front and a full clause after.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each, name the link first: time, cause, condition or comment. That chooses the connector.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Find the plain twin
activities.instructions:
Write the plain twin of each.
1. notwithstanding  2. pursuant to  3. aforementioned  4. herewith
5. therein  6. prior to  7. in the event of  8. refrain from
Now answer.
9. Which word in this unit has NO plain twin, and why?
10. Rewrite for a letter: 'Pursuant to the aforementioned agreement, and
    notwithstanding the obligations therein, notice is hereby given.'
11. Why is 'I hereby went to the meeting' impossible?
activities.answers:
1. despite  2. under  3. that, or the  4. with this  5. in it  6. before
7. if  8. do not
9. hereby. It makes the saying itself the act, and no plain word does that.
10. Under that agreement, and despite the obligations in it, notice is hereby given.
11. hereby only works where the sentence PERFORMS the act. You cannot perform a
    past action by saying it now.
9 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the plain twin beside each. If it says the same thing, it is the better word.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Rewrite the unreadable letter
activities.instructions:
Here is a letter that is entirely correct and almost unreadable.
Rewrite it so that somebody reading it once knows what to do.
Keep dials 1 to 3 up. Bring dials 4 and 5 down. Keep hereby if it earns its place.

'Pursuant to the aforementioned correspondence, and notwithstanding the
obligations set out therein, the undersigned is constrained to advise that,
the requisite documentation not having been furnished within the period
specified, the application referenced above has been placed in abeyance,
in which circumstance the applicant is hereby given notice that closure
will follow in the absence of receipt within thirty days.'
activities.answers:
Yours will differ. A good version has all five of these.
1. It is split into at least three sentences.
2. It says you, not the applicant or the undersigned.
3. It keeps the passive where blame is not the point: has been placed on hold.
4. It keeps hereby, because the sentence gives notice.
5. A reader knows what to supply and by when.
A model: 'We have not received the documents we asked for. Your application has
therefore been placed on hold. Please supply them within thirty days. I hereby
give notice that the application will otherwise be closed.'
Score yourself out of five. Four or more: good.
activities.solo: Underline every word you would not say aloud to the reader. Replace each one.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the letter
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. What is the reference number, and by when must the documents be supplied?
2. What happens if they cannot be supplied by that date?
3. Has a decision been taken?
4. Copy two present perfect passives and say what each reports.
5. Copy the past perfect passive and say what it is earlier than.
6. Copy the sentence with hereby and say why that word is doing real work.
7. Is the closing correct for the opening?
activities.answers:
1. HA-2291; by 30 April.
2. Notify them in writing, and the file is held open for a further month.
3. No, and none will be until the file is complete.
4. 'Your application has been received' and 'has been referred to the assessment
   team.' Both report a position without promising action.
5. 'No further correspondence had been received' — earlier than the review on 2 April.
6. 'I hereby confirm that the application will not be closed before 30 May.'
   The sentence IS the confirmation; it is the one commitment in the letter.
7. Yes. It opens with a name, so Yours sincerely is right.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Read the letter with a pen and underline every has been and had been before you answer.

quizzes.q: Which change turns the dial that does the MOST damage when overdone?
options: we received it -> it has been received
quizzes.why: Distance from the reader is dial five, and turning it up makes a letter cold. The first three are cheap and usually improve official writing.

options: clear English, which may also be formal
quizzes.a: clear English, which may also be formal
quizzes.why: A document can be entirely formal and still be understood the first time. Plain is about clarity, not about register.
Without been the sentence says the application did the receiving. The been is what gets dropped, exactly as in Unit 10.

quizzes.q: Which of these commits somebody to doing something?
options: Your application will be considered on 14 August.
quizzes.a: Your application will be considered on 14 August.
quizzes.why: The first three report a state and commit nobody. A date is what turns an acknowledgement into an answer.

quizzes.q: No reply ___ when the matter was escalated.
quizzes.why: The absence of a reply was already true when the escalation happened, so the past perfect. had received would say the reply did the receiving.

quizzes.q: In a formal account, what does the present perfect report?
quizzes.why: The three layers are past perfect for what was already true, past simple for the events, and present perfect for the current position.

quizzes.q: The parts may be delayed, ___ the work will be rescheduled.
quizzes.why: It is a condition, not a moment or a cause. in which case means if that turns out to be so.

quizzes.q: No reply came by the 14th, ___ the matter was escalated.
quizzes.why: The link is a moment in time. as a result of which would claim the silence caused the escalation, which is a bigger claim.

quizzes.q: The plain twin of 'pursuant to' is:
quizzes.why: Pursuant to clause 6 and under clause 6 mean the same thing, and one of them can be read by the person it applies to.

quizzes.q: Which word has no plain twin?
quizzes.why: hereby makes the saying itself the act. The other three all have everyday equivalents: despite, that, and in it.

quizzes.q: Why is 'I hereby went to the meeting' impossible?
options: hereby is too formal for that verb.
hereby only works where the sentence performs the act.
quizzes.a: hereby only works where the sentence performs the act.
quizzes.why: I hereby confirm IS the confirmation. You cannot perform a past action by saying it now.

quizzes.q: A letter opens 'Dear Ms Okonkwo'. How should it close?
quizzes.why: Sincerely follows a named person; faithfully follows Dear Sir or Madam. The pair is a British convention and it is noticed.

teacherNotes.note: All three use codes are increments into REGISTER rather than into new form: 9Ug.05 and 9Ug.07 are perfect passives built in Units 9 and 10, and 9Us.02 is the clause-which from Unit 1. Cards 1 and 5 serve 9Wca.03, style and register appropriate to a genre, which is what holds the unit together.
Card 3 needs the past perfect passive from Unit 10 and the three-layer chronology from Unit 9. Card 4 needs Unit 1's clause-which, and will not make sense to a learner who has not met it.

The dropped been is the same error as in Unit 10, and it recurs here because the forms are longer: 'has been referred' has two weak syllables before the main word. Speaking 2 drills it for that reason.
Learners who meet the formal connectors put them in emails, where they are too heavy. Practice 4 item 8 asks them to say so explicitly, and the answer is 'all of them'.
The sincerely / faithfully pair is a British convention, and getting it wrong is noticed in Britain and almost nowhere else. The word entries say so rather than presenting it as a universal rule.

This unit argues against a way of writing that many learners have been taught is correct and professional. It does so with evidence rather than assertion: Reading 1 gives the eight-tenant test, and the original letter is described as entirely correct. The lesson is that correctness and readability are separate, not that formal writing is bad.

Practice 6 is the unit's real assessment: an unreadable but entirely correct letter to rebuild. It is marked on five structural criteria including whether hereby is kept, because keeping the one word that earns its place is harder than deleting all of them.

selfAssessment.statement: I know formality is five dials rather than one switch.
I keep sentence length and distance from the reader low, even in formal writing.
I can acknowledge something in the present perfect passive.
I know that an acknowledgement promises nothing until it carries a date.
I never drop the been from has been or had been.
I can use in which case, at which point and for which reason correctly.
I can give the plain twin of notwithstanding, pursuant to and aforementioned.
I know why hereby has no plain twin.

assignment.title: The letter, tested on a reader
assignment.instructions:
Part one. Write a formal letter of about 180 words conveying a decision somebody
will not like. Open with a name and close correctly.
Use the present perfect passive at least three times and the past perfect passive
at least twice. Use at least two formal which connectors. Use hereby exactly once,
and only where the sentence performs an act.
No sentence may run past about twenty-five words.
Part two. Write the same letter again with all five dials at maximum: long sentences,
the undersigned, and every formal word you know. It must still be entirely correct.
Part three. Give both versions to somebody and ask them, without help, what each one
requires them to do and by when.
Write four lines on what they got right and wrong in each, and what you would change.
If nobody is available, mark both yourself against three questions: what must be
supplied, by when, and what happens otherwise.
assignment.submissionType: Two versions of a letter and a reader's test
